The lot of life which permits making the third libation, i.e., which is under the protection of Διὸς σωτῆρος [Zeus the savior], to whom the third libation was made, perfect happiness, as Blomfield explained, who collected more about this libation, among which the scholium on Plato's Philebus p. 95 a: τρίτον τῷ σωτῆρι [the third to the savior]: it is said by metaphor from the custom in drinking parties. Sophocles in Nauplius Katapleon (fr. 375): ἐκιρνῶντο γὰρ ἐν αὐταῖς κρατῆρες τρεῖς, καὶ τὸν μὲν πρῶτον Διὸς Ὀλυμπίου καὶ θεῶν Ὀλυμπίων ἔλεγον, τὸν δὲ δεύτερον ἡρώων, τὸν δὲ τρίτον σωτῆρος [for three bowls were mixed in them, and the first they called of Olympian Zeus and the Olympian gods, the second of heroes, and the third of the savior]. Aeschylus refers to it in the passages cited under τρίτος [third]: Ag. 1386, Ch. 244, 578, 1073, Eum. 759, Suppl. 27, Fr. 52.
With pure, unyoked voice she honored the third-libation, fortunate life of her dear father.

Schuetz rightly: 'τὸ μὲν πίτνον κῦμα [the falling wave] designates the calamity of Oedipus himself, but that κύμα [wave], which is described by these words ἄλλο δ᾽ ἀείρει [another raises] etc., pertains to the war stirred up between his sons.'
